name: Vaxholm Fortress

opening_hours.seasonal_note: Open daily mid-May to mid-September only. Reached by boat from Vaxholm town or direct from Stockholm.

accessibility: Limited — boat access required; interiors involve stairs
tagline: The guardian of Stockholm — a Renaissance sea fortress on its own island in the archipelago
highlights: Built by Gustav Vasa to protect Stockholm from seaborne invasion
Dramatically positioned on its own island in the Stockholm Archipelago
Reached exclusively by boat — the approach by water is spectacular
National Coastal Defence Museum inside the fortress
The fortress that stopped a Russian fleet in 1719
description: Vaxholm Fortress is the guardian of Stockholm — a Renaissance sea fortress on its own island in the inner Stockholm Archipelago, commanding the main waterway between the Baltic and the Swedish capital. Founded by King Gustav Vasa in 1548, the fortress was continuously expanded and reinforced for 350 years as Sweden's primary coastal defence against seaborne attack. It was never taken by force: a Russian fleet turned back from its walls in 1719 during the Great Northern War, one of the most significant moments in the fortress's long history. Today it is home to the National Coastal Defence Museum, with collections spanning Swedish naval and coastal military history. The fortress is only accessible by boat — a 10-minute crossing from Vaxholm town, itself a charming wooden-housed island community 35 km from Stockholm, making the whole excursion one of the finest summer day trips from the Swedish capital.
history: Gustav Vasa ordered the fortress built in 1548 to protect Stockholm from seaborne attack. It was expanded in the 17th century during Sweden's era as a Baltic great power, with Vauban-influenced bastions added. In 1719 a Russian fleet under Admiral Apraxin turned back from the fortress during Peter the Great's retaliatory raids on the Swedish coast. The fortress continued as an active military installation until 1833, when the navy moved to Karlskrona. It was converted to a museum in the 20th century.
how_to_visit:
**Getting there:** The fortress sits on its own island and is only reachable by boat. From Stockholm, take the Waxholmsbolaget ferry from Strömkajen or Nybroplan to Vaxholm town (about 1 hour through the inner archipelago); from Vaxholm harbour a local boat crosses to the fortress island in around 10 minutes. Alternatively, drive to Vaxholm (35 km from Stockholm, about 40 minutes) and catch the local boat from the town quay. The ferry approach through the archipelago is worth the journey in itself.

**Tickets:** Walk-up entry SEK 100 adult, SEK 50 child. The GYG tour (t635141, from €149, 4.5★/43 reviews) is a guided small-group day trip from Stockholm covering Vaxholm and the archipelago, combining boat travel and a fortress visit with guided commentary — book in advance.

**Practical tips:** The fortress is only open mid-May to mid-September — plan around this seasonal window. Arrive in Vaxholm with enough time to explore the town's 19th-century wooden architecture and waterfront before or after crossing to the island; the seafood restaurants on the main square are very good. Wear layers — the waterway between the town and fortress is exposed to the wind even in summer.

**Combine with:** [Stockholm Royal Palace](/castles/sweden/stockholm-royal-palace) in Gamla Stan for a full Stockholm royal history day, or [Gripsholm Castle](/castles/sweden/gripsholm-castle) as a second Lake Mälaren fortress for a longer Sweden castle circuit.

faqs.question: Can I drive to Vaxholm Fortress?
faqs.answer: You can drive to Vaxholm town (35 km from Stockholm), but the fortress is on a separate island accessible only by boat from the town harbour.

faqs.question: What is the Coastal Defence Museum?
faqs.answer: A museum inside the fortress covering Swedish coastal and naval defence history from the 16th century to the 20th, with artillery, weapons, uniforms, and ship models.

faqs.question: Is Vaxholm worth visiting beyond the fortress?
faqs.answer: Yes — the town of Vaxholm has beautiful 19th-century wooden architecture, good seafood restaurants, and is the gateway to the Stockholm Archipelago boat routes further out to sea.
